Expurgation is the act of deliberately removing parts of a written work, speech, film, or any other piece of content that someone considers offensive, immoral, inappropriate, or unsuitable — before that content is published or made available to an audience.

Think of it like this: imagine someone takes a famous novel, goes through it with a red pen, crosses out every passage they find too vulgar, too sexual, too violent, or too controversial, and then publishes that "cleaned-up" version. That entire process — the reviewing, the cutting, the sanitizing — is called expurgation.

The key idea is that the work itself survives, but pieces of it are deliberately erased on moral or social grounds.

If you expurgate something, you purge (remove/get rid of) content that is considered impure, harmful, or objectionable. So expurgation = the act of that purging. It is not about improving writing quality, fixing errors, or changing the story's direction. It is purely about removing content someone has decided is unfit for the intended audience.
What kind of content gets removed?

The content targeted in expurgation typically falls into these categories:

  • Sexual or explicit content — passages describing sex, nudity, or anything considered obscene
  • Profanity and vulgar language — swear words, crude expressions
  • Blasphemous content — material considered disrespectful to religion or God
  • Politically dangerous ideas — views that authorities or publishers want suppressed
  • Excessively violent descriptions
  • Content deemed harmful to children — material considered too adult or morally corrupting for young readers

Expurgation can be carried out by several kinds of people or institutions, each with different motivations:

Publishers and editors might expurgate a book to make it commercially safe — to sell it in schools, conservative markets, or to a broader family audience.

Governments and authorities might order expurgation to remove political content they consider dangerous or subversive.

Religious institutions have historically expurgated texts to remove content they considered sinful or doctrinally threatening.

Authors themselves sometimes expurgate their own earlier works under social pressure, though this is less common.

The motivation can be protective (shielding children from adult content), political (controlling information), commercial (reaching wider audiences), or moral/religious (enforcing community standards).

The most well-known case of expurgation in literary history involves a man named Thomas Bowdler, who in 1807 published a version of Shakespeare's plays called The Family Shakespeare. He went through every play and removed or altered every line he thought was inappropriate for women and children — sexual references, crude jokes, morally difficult passages. What remained was a sanitized version of Shakespeare, stripped of much of its complexity and edge.

His act of expurgation was so famous — and so extreme — that it gave birth to a whole new English word: bowdlerize, which is now a widely used synonym for expurgation (and usually carries a tone of mockery or disapproval).
Expurgation vs. things that seem similar

These distinctions are important because learners often confuse expurgation with nearby concepts:

Expurgation vs. Censorship:
Censorship is broader. It can mean banning an entire work, preventing its publication altogether, or suppressing a topic. Expurgation is a specific type of censorship — it targets and removes parts of a work while allowing the rest to survive. All expurgation involves a degree of censorship, but not all censorship is expurgation.

Expurgation vs. Editing:
Ordinary editing improves clarity, fixes grammar, strengthens structure, and refines style. Expurgation has nothing to do with quality. Its only concern is moral or social acceptability. An editor might cut a chapter because it's poorly written; an expurgator cuts it because it's considered offensive.

Expurgation vs. Abridgement:
Abridgement means shortening a work — removing content to make it shorter or more accessible, without a specific moral agenda. An abridged novel is a condensed version. An expurgated novel is a morally filtered version.

Expurgation is genuinely controversial, and understanding both sides will give you a fuller sense of how the word is used in the real world.

Those who defend expurgation argue that it makes important works accessible to audiences who would otherwise be excluded — particularly children — and that some content truly is harmful or gratuitous. They see expurgation as a responsible, protective act.

Those who criticize expurgation argue that it distorts the original author's vision and intent, strips works of their authenticity, and is ultimately a form of intellectual dishonesty. A sanitized Shakespeare is not really Shakespeare. They often see expurgation as a sign of intellectual cowardice or authoritarian control, and the word in modern usage frequently carries a negative connotation — implying that something valuable has been wrongly removed.

In most contemporary usage, calling something an "act of expurgation" subtly implies disapproval — a sense that the cuts were unnecessary, damaging to the original, or driven by prudishness.
How it appears in a sentence

• The expurgation of the novel's most powerful chapters left readers with a hollow, toothless version of the story.
  • The government ordered the expurgation of all politically critical passages before the book could be sold in the country.
  • The publisher's expurgation of the memoir was driven entirely by fear of controversy, not by any concern for literary merit.
  • Scholars studying the original manuscript were disturbed by how much had been lost to decades of expurgation.
Expurgation is the act of cutting out parts of a work considered offensive or inappropriate, producing a "cleaner" but often compromised version of the original.
